versions.text:
Tom and Jerry in Venice

Tom was a small cat with a big wish. He wanted to ride a gondola. Not just any gondola, but one that glided through the canals of Venice, the city of water.

"We will sneak aboard," Tom whispered to his friend Jerry. "Nobody will notice two tiny mice."

Jerry was a mouse. He was not tiny at all, but he liked to think he was very clever.

Hmm, let me set this right. Tom is the one who wants to ride, and Jerry is his friend. Tom is a cat, and the story needs a cat with a ridiculous wish. Here it is again, told properly.

Tom and Jerry in Venice

Tom was a small gray cat with a big, silly wish. He wanted to ride a gondola through the canals of Venice. The canals were wide, green, and wobbly with light.

"We will sneak aboard," Tom whispered to his friend Jerry. "Nobody will notice two of us hiding under a striped cushion."

Jerry was a little brown mouse with round ears. He nodded, though his whiskers trembled. "Sneaking is my favorite thing," he said, which was not quite true.

They crept down the stone steps to the water. A gondola bobbed there, black and shining, with a bright red cushion. Its gondolier stood at the back. He had a curly mustache and a hat with a feather.

"Now!" whispered Tom. They tiptoed onto the boat and dived under the cushion.

The gondolier stopped rowing. He tapped the boat with his oar. Tap, tap, tap. "Aha! Stowaways!" he said. "Before you ride my gondola, you must learn to sing opera. Everyone knows that is the rule."

"Opera?" squeaked Jerry.

"Opera!" sang the gondolier, and he flung his arms wide. "La la LAAA!"

Tom tried first. He opened his mouth and let out a sound like a squeaky gate. "Mrrr-OW-ahhh!"

The gondolier clapped his hands over his ears. "Not quite, my furry friend. Again!"

Tom puffed out his chest and tried again, even louder. "MEEEOOOW-ROOO-LAAAA!" A pigeon fell off the railing. A lady on the bridge dropped her ice cream. Jerry hid behind the cushion.

"Too loud!" cried the gondolier, wiping his eyes. "Now, the little one. You try."

Jerry took a deep breath. He sang in a teeny voice. "Eee-eee-ooo-eee!" It sounded like a kettle that had just started to boil.

"Better," said the gondolier, "but still not opera!"

Tom had an idea. He pulled out a wooden spoon from his bag and tapped it on the side of the boat. Tonk, tonk, tonkety-tonk! Jerry joined in with a squeak. Squeek-squeek, squeek-squeek! Together they made a silly, rattling tune.

The gondolier's mustache began to wiggle. Then his shoulders began to bounce. Then he threw back his head and laughed so hard that his feather flew off his hat and landed in the water.

"Ha ha! That is the most ridiculous opera I have ever heard!" he chuckled. "Hop in, both of you. You have earned your ride!"

Tom and Jerry cheered and scrambled onto the red cushion. The gondolier rowed them along the canal. Water lapped against the boat, soft and slow. Lanterns glowed on the old pink palaces. Somewhere a violin played a gentle song.

The gondolier hummed as he rowed. The boat rocked, back and forth, back and forth. Tom's eyes grew heavy. Jerry curled up beside him, his tail wrapped around his nose.

"Goodnight, canal," whispered Tom.

"Goodnight, gondolier," murmured Jerry.

The gondolier smiled and rowed on, quiet now, as the boat drifted under the bridges of Venice. The city of water settled into sleep, and so did two tired friends, safe and warm on a red cushion.

The end.
